raw_case_text:
Our patient is a 28-year-old male from Gaza who was transferred to our hospital's medical intensive care unit (ICU) because of complicated leptospirosis. His past surgical and medical history was insignificant. Ten days before admission, the patient had a rat bite in his left big toe, so he sought medical advice, where he was given a tetanus vaccine and discharged with a recommendation to follow up at the infectious clinic. Later on, the patient started complaining of nonspecific symptoms of headache, general weakness, and myalgia, for which he took analgesics. However, his symptoms worsened, and he started to notice a yellowish discoloration all over his body, associated with fever. So, he was admitted to the medical ward in Gaza, where Investigations were performed and confirmed the diagnosis of leptospirosis. Those revealed alveolar hemorrhage, cholestatic jaundice, and acute kidney injury. The patient's condition rapidly deteriorated, requiring intubation and urgent transfer to our hospital for Advanced ICU management.
Upon arrival, the Patient was admitted to the ICU immediately. On examination, He was deeply sedated on mechanical ventilation SIMV, PEEP:10, FIO2: 100%, PS:20, RR:18). He was pale, deeply jaundiced, and ecchymosis was found on his hands and legs. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral basal crepitation. His vital signs showed a heart rate of 88 beats/min, blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg, and body temperature of 38.6 C. His blood oxygen saturation was 99% on the parameters as mentioned above. Upon admission, extensive laboratory investigations were obtained, including a full septic workup (Table 1). Arterial blood gases revealed a PH of 7.40, CO2:45.3 mmHG, and HCO3:28 mEq/L. The white blood cell count was elevated, primarily the neutrophils. He was anemic, and thrombocytopenia was present. The transaminases level was average. There was a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine levels were significantly increased, suggesting acute renal injury. Urine analysis showed no proteinuria. CT scan showed diffuse bilateral areas of patchy alveolar infiltration ground glass opacities, representing alveolar hemorrhage (Figure 1). The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, including vancomycin, meropenem, and doxycycline, as well as esomeprazole 40 mg orally and a Pulse dose of Methylprednisolone 1 g once daily for three days, then tapering gradually to 80 g. By the sixth day of admission, the patient developed Ventilator-associated pneumonia. Sputum culture showed pseudomonas aeruginosa sensitive for colistin.
Day by day, the Patient's condition dramatically resolved. His labs showed stable blood hemostasis The creatinine, liver enzymes, bilirubin, and CRP gradually subsided. Also, his respiratory conditions improved. The patient was successfully extubated on day 10 from admission. His condition was stable, and he was transferred to the medical ward to continue antibiotics therapy. On day 18 of admission, he suddenly developed abdominal pain and severe hematemesis of a large amount of blood (about 3 liters). He became unconscious with a GCC scale of 4/15; the blood pressure was unrecordable. An Urgent resuscitative strategy for hemorrhagic shock was started, including the following: two bores IV cannula, two central lines (femoral and internal jugular), massive blood product transfusion with a total of 30 units (10 units of PRBC, 10 FFP, 10 PLTS), several liters of IV Fluid (Normal saline and ringer lactate), and calcium gluconate administration. Then Intubation was done, and adrenaline and noradrenaline were started. An urgent upper endoscopy revealed an intact oesophagus and a stomach full of blood. Laboratory results showed a Hb of 4.22 mg/dl, HCT of 15.7%, MCH of 27 PG/ML, MCV of 88 microm3, RBC of 1.4 x 106/microl, wbc of 11 x 103/L, Platelets of 50 x 103/micro, SGPT of 94 U/L, SGOT of 37 U/L, BUN of 28 mg/dl, Cre of 0.9 mg/dl, Fibrinogen of 220 mg/dl, CRP of 12.4 mg/dl, D-dimer of 910 mg/dl, PT of 13.6, INR of 1.15, APTT of 20.6, T. bilirubin of 2 mg/dl, and D. Bilirubin of 1.3 mg/dl.
The patient underwent urgent exploratory laparotomy. Open stomach anterior wall and gastric lumen packing were done. The upper half of the mucosa of the stomach oozed fresh blood, and a Splenic artery aneurysm eroded into the gastroesophageal junction. So left gastric artery was ligated, Splenectomy and proximal partial gastrectomy with distal esophagectomy were performed. Intraoperatively, the Patient receives 8 PRPC, 10 FFP, 10 PLT,2500-unit prothrombin complex concentration, and 8,000 CC IV fluid. Afterward, the Patient was readmitted to the ICU, fully sedated and intubated. The next day, a second look procedure was done involving esophagogastric anastomosis and anterior continues repair of the wall. A jejunostomy feeding tube along with abdominal drains was applied. Figure 2 Showed the Patient's clinical course during the first 23 days of hospitalization.
5-6 days later, the Patient complained of shortness of breath and chest pain. A physical exam revealed tachypnea, desaturation, crackles on the right side, and decreased breath sounds on the left side. A portable chest x-ray showed pleural effusion and left-sided pneumothorax. CT scan findings were: Collapsed left lung due to complete obstruction of the left main bronchus. Mild to moderate left-sided pneumothorax, mild bilateral pleural effusion. A focal consolidation area is seen at the right lower lobe with surrounding ground glass opacities. Two Chest tubes were inserted at the left side, and the Patient's condition improved (Figure 3). The Patient underwent a bronchoscopy, which showed a left main bronchus occlusion. Multiple bronchoscopies were performed by which large amounts of secretions were removed.
The Patient developed an unresolved fever. Full septic work was done, and Antibiotics were upgraded. Chest and abdomen Ct scan with contrast revealed a right upper lobe cavitary lesion surrounded by ground glass opacities. Multiple intraabdominal fluid collections were noted (Figure 4). Ultrasound Guidance drainage was done. Fluid culture revealed stenotrophomonas bacteria sensitive for colistin, levofloxacin, and resprim. The patient was given Colistin and resprim.
Day by day, the Patient showed gradual resolution of his status and was successfully extubated. Extensive supportive strategies were followed for recovery from critical illness, including exercise rehabilitation and physiotherapy. He was transferred to the medical world and discharged home. On follow up the patient was in a good general condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presenting with headache, general weakness, myalgia, jaundice, and fever progressing to respiratory failure and multiorgan dysfunction following a rat bite 10 days prior.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to admission, the patient sustained a rat bite on his left big toe, for which he received a tetanus vaccine. Subsequently, he developed headache, generalized weakness, and myalgias managed with analgesics. His symptoms progressively worsened with high fever and generalized yellowish skin discoloration. He was initially hospitalized in a local medical ward where alveolar hemorrhage, cholestatic jaundice, and acute kidney injury were identified. His condition deteriorated rapidly, requiring endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and urgent transfer to the intensive care unit.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical and surgical history was insignificant. Epidemiological exposure includes a rat bite to the left big toe 10 days before admission. Prior therapy included tetanus vaccination and analgesics.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports headache, generalized weakness, and diffuse myalgias. Home medications: analgesics. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon ICU admission: deeply sedated on mechanical ventilation (SIMV mode, PEEP 10 cmH2O, FiO2 100%, PS 20 cmH2O, RR 18 breaths/min). Heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, body temperature 38.6 °C, blood oxygen saturation 99%. General: pale, deeply jaundiced, with ecchymoses on hands and legs. Respiratory: bilateral basal crepitations on chest auscultation. On day 18: Glasgow Coma Scale 4/15 with unrecordable blood pressure during acute hemorrhage. On day 23: tachypneic and desaturating, with right-sided crackles and decreased left-sided breath sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gases on admission: pH 7.40, PaCO2 45.3 mmHg, HCO3 28 mEq/L. Complete blood count showed elevated white blood cell count (predominantly neutrophils), anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Biochemistry: normal transaminases, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and significantly elevated blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine. Urinalysis: no proteinuria. Day 18 hemorrhage labs: Hb 4.22 mg/dL, HCT 15.7%, MCH 27 pg/mL, MCV 88 mcm^3, RBC 1.4 x 10^6/mcL, WBC 11 x 10^3/L, platelets 50 x 10^3/mcL, SGPT 94 U/L, SGOT 37 U/L, BUN 28 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, fibrinogen 220 mg/dL, CRP 12.4 mg/dL, D-dimer 910 mg/dL, PT 13.6 s, INR 1.15, APTT 20.6 s, total bilirubin 2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL. Portable chest X-ray: pleural effusion and left-sided pneumothorax.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial chest CT: diffuse bilateral areas of patchy alveolar infiltration and ground-glass opacities consistent with alveolar hemorrhage. Urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: intact esophagus and stomach full of blood. Diagnostic bronchoscopy: left main bronchus occlusion by copious secretions. Contrast chest and abdominal CT: collapsed left lung due to complete obstruction of the left main bronchus, mild-to-moderate left pneumothorax, mild bilateral pleural effusion, focal consolidation in right lower lobe with surrounding ground-glass opacities, right upper lobe cavitary lesion surrounded by ground-glass opacities, and multiple intra-abdominal fluid collections. Exploratory laparotomy: upper gastric mucosal bleeding and a splenic artery aneurysm eroding into the gastroesophageal junction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Complicated leptospirosis (Weil's disease) presenting with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, cholestatic jaundice, and acute kidney injury following a rat bite, confirmed by investigations in Gaza. Hospitalization was complicated by ventilator-associated pneumonia secondary to Pseudomonas aeruginosa (sensitive to colistin), massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage from a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm eroding into the gastroesophageal junction, complete left main bronchus obstruction with lung collapse, left pneumothorax, and secondary intra-abdominal fluid collection infection with Stenotrophomonas (sensitive to colistin, levofloxacin, and resprim/co-trimoxazole).
Plan & Management: Initial broad-spectrum coverage with vancomycin, meropenem, and doxycycline, alongside esomeprazole 40 mg PO and pulse methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 days tapered to 80 mg. Emergent massive resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock (30 blood product units: 10 PRBC, 10 FFP, 10 platelets; IV fluids, calcium gluconate, adrenaline, noradrenaline) and exploratory laparotomy with splenic artery aneurysm ligation, splenectomy, proximal partial gastrectomy, distal esophagectomy, and subsequent second-look esophagogastric reconstruction with jejunostomy feeding tube. Left chest tube thoracostomy and therapeutic bronchoscopies. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous abdominal drainage with targeted colistin and resprim antimicrobial therapy. Physical therapy and rehabilitation. Successful extubation, resolution of organ failure, and discharge home in good general condition.
